title: Does each ton of wheat cost the same?
hook: The first ton of wheat costs 1 ton of corn. What does the tenth cost?

knows: opportunity cost: making more of one thing means making less of another
how to read a curve on a graph
doesNotKnow: that trading one good for another often gets steeper as you push one side
why a production frontier bows outward

misconception: Moving from corn to wheat always costs the same corn per ton.
objective: The learner can read the corn given up for each extra ton of wheat off a bowed frontier, and explain that it grows because resources are not equally suited to both goods.

claims.text: On this made-up farm (frontier corn = 100 − wheat², not shown to the learner), switching the first field to wheat (0 to 1 ton) costs 1 ton of corn, and switching the last (9 to 10 tons) costs 19.
claims.source: corn(0) − corn(1) = 100 − 99 = 1; corn(9) − corn(10) = 19 − 0 = 19. Demo.tsx stepCost(). | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v2, wave D r5 revision by demo-builder): learner-visible sentence changed; needs a fresh check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): corn(w) = 100 - w^2: stepCost(1) = 1, stepCost(10) = 19; the formula appears in neither the question nor the chip (Demo.tsx v2).

claims.text: The corn lost per ton runs 1, 3, 5, … 19, growing by 2 each step.

The frontier bends because the fields are not all alike: the first wheat goes on the field worst for corn (it grew 1 ton of corn), the last takes the best corn field (19), and each drop on the staircase is the corn its field used to grow (increasing opportunity cost).
claims.source: Bowed-out production possibilities frontier and increasing opportunity cost (N. G. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 2 'Thinking Like an Economist', the production possibilities frontier). | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v2, wave D r5 revision by demo-builder): learner-visible sentence changed; needs a fresh check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Model part checked in Demo.tsx: field strip k shows stepCost(k) = 2k - 1, turned to wheat in order 1..10, so each drop equals that field's corn. The general principle (bowed-out PPF because resources are not equally suited) is corroborated by secondary search-result text; Mankiw ch. 2 not opened. The learner sentence is about the farm on screen, so it does not depend on the unopened source.

claims.text: The curve is made up to show the shape, not data from a real farm.
claims.source: Stage chip 'Made-up farm'; reveal's last line.

claims.text: The made-up farm has 10 fields, each able to grow 1 ton of wheat or, from worst to best for corn, 1, 3, 5, … 19 tons of corn; wheat is put on the fields worst for corn first, which gives the frontier corn = 100 − wheat².
claims.source: The lesson's own model in Demo.tsx (field strip: field k grows stepCost(k) = 2k − 1 corn; sum of the first n is n², so corn = 100 − n²). The ordering 'worst for corn first' is what a farm maximising output would do (standard textbook account of a bowed-out PPF, e.g. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 2; chapter not re-checked). | Added 2026-10-14 (v2) by demo-builder. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): sum of 2k - 1 for k = 1..n is n^2, so corn = 100 - n^2. Worst-for-corn first is output-maximising: every field gives 1 ton of wheat, so switching the field with least corn minimises corn lost. Chip 'Made-up farm: 10 fields, worst to best for corn' matches.

recall.question: A town turns its factories from making bikes to making scooters. The first 100 scooters cost 50 bikes. What usually happens to the cost of the last 100 scooters?
recall.why: The first switch uses the factories best at scooters and worst at bikes. The last switch takes the best bike factories, so each extra scooter costs more bikes.
